title: Modules and packages: organize code without confusion
masterChecklist: Imports, import forms, import-time effects, module cache, sys.path, dir, __name__
User modules, packages, __init__.py, relative imports, namespace packages, public API design
whyItMatters: As a program grows, one file becomes hard to test and navigate. Modules separate related jobs; packages group modules into a meaningful project structure.
simpleExplanation: A module is a Python file that can be imported. A package is a directory used to group modules. import runs a module the first time it is loaded in a process, then Python usually reuses the loaded module from its cache. __name__ lets a file distinguish being run directly from being imported.
mentalModel: A module is one labelled drawer; a package is a cabinet containing related drawers. Importing opens the drawer so you can use its labelled tools.
outcomes: Import a standard module and a local module.
Describe why import-time work should be small and predictable.
Choose a package boundary based on responsibility.

realWorldExample.scenario: A study application separates score calculations, file loading, and screen messages into different modules.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: Code that reads files or starts a server during import makes tests and reuse surprising. Circular imports can occur when modules know too much about each other.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Keep imports near the top, avoid side effects during import, expose a small public API, and put command-line startup under a main guard.

workedExample.code:
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    root = Path(folder)
    (root / 'score_tools.py').write_text('def passed(score):\n    return score >= 70\n', encoding='utf-8')
    (root / 'app.py').write_text("from score_tools import passed\nif __name__ == '__main__':\n    print(passed(82))\n", encoding='utf-8')
    run = subprocess.run([sys.executable, str(root / 'app.py')], cwd=root, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
    print(run.stdout.strip())
explanation: The temporary folder creates two real Python files rather than pretending comments separate files in one editor.
score_tools.py owns the calculation and app.py imports it by name.
Running app.py as a child process executes its main guard and prints the result.
TemporaryDirectory removes the practice files afterward; importing the helper itself has no demo side effect.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Change the score to 69 inside app.py and predict False. Keep this a local disposable experiment.

procedure: Create score_tools.py and app.py in the same folder.
Import passed in a temporary test file.
Move related modules into a package directory as the project grows.
Do not modify sys.path as a casual workaround; fix the project layout or execution method instead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting large actions at module top level.
commonMistakes.why: They happen during import, surprising tests and other callers.
commonMistakes.avoid: Put startup work in a function and call it under a main guard.

commonMistakes.why: It hides where names came from and can overwrite local names.
commonMistakes.avoid: Import the specific public names you use, or import the module and qualify its names.

commonMistakes.why: Each module waits for a partially initialized other module.
commonMistakes.avoid: Move shared concepts to a lower-level module or redesign the dependency direction.

lab.title: Split a score helper into a module
lab.safety: The self-contained lab creates two uniquely named files in a temporary local folder; no network or existing project file changes.
lab.starterCode:
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

# In a temporary folder, write score_tools.py and app.py.
# Put grade_label in score_tools.py and the guarded print in app.py.
# Run app.py with sys.executable and print its output.
guidedSteps: Create a TemporaryDirectory for the two practice files.
Write score_tools.py with grade_label(score), returning pass or review.
Write app.py with a named import and a main guard.
Run app.py using sys.executable and cwd set to the temporary folder.
Print captured output and test score 69 as a safe experiment.
checks: The helper module does not print during import.
The application file has a main guard.
The actual two-file import runs and prints pass for 82.
hints: Use from score_tools import grade_label inside app.py.
Use subprocess.run with sys.executable and capture_output=True.
lab.solution:
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    root = Path(folder)
    (root / 'score_tools.py').write_text("def grade_label(score):\n    return 'pass' if score >= 70 else 'review'\n", encoding='utf-8')
    (root / 'app.py').write_text("from score_tools import grade_label\nif __name__ == '__main__':\n    print(grade_label(82))\n", encoding='utf-8')
    run = subprocess.run([sys.executable, str(root / 'app.py')], cwd=root, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
    print(run.stdout.strip())
lab.solutionExplanation: Real temporary files make the named import executable in one editor session. The calculation is reusable because importing it does not run the guarded application interface.
challenges: Find the bug: print inside grade_label instead of return. What does a caller receive?
Experiment: import score_tools twice. Why should the module avoid important repeated side effects?

projectConnection.milestone: Separate report calculations, input reading, and command-line startup into dedicated modules.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: You can show which file owns each responsibility and run the app without triggering work merely by importing a helper.

assessment.question: What is a Python module?
assessment.answer: A Python file that can define and provide code to other files through import.
assessment.explanation: Modules are a basic unit of code organization.

assessment.question: Why use if __name__ == '__main__'?
assessment.answer: To run entry-point work only when that file is executed directly.
assessment.explanation: It keeps importing the module from unexpectedly starting the application.

assessment.question: Why avoid import *?
assessment.answer: It makes name origins unclear and can cause collisions.
